articles.title: On the bubble? Giants WR Odell Beckham Jr., Steelers RB Kaleb Johnson among those who might not make 53-man roster
articles.summary: Here are some of the notable names that could be in danger of being cut or perhaps traded as teams finalize their regular-season rosters.
articles.body:
It's not a comfortable time of year for many NFL players.

On Sunday, teams must cut down their rosters to 53 players. That makes for some tough decisions. It also has front offices scouring the bottoms of rosters, trying to find intriguing players they might want to pick up if they're cut, or acquire in trades just before the roster deadline.

Here are some of the notable names that could be in danger of being cut or perhaps traded as teams get down to 53 players:

Calvin Austin III's season-ending knee injury could help Beckham, who is trying to complete a cool comeback story with the Giants. Beckham hasn't played for the Giants since 2018, and didn't play at all last season. He got a shot at age 33 to make the team. He has had some fun throwback highlights in camp

Still, the Giants aren't making decisions based on nostalgia. Does Beckham fit in their receiver room? He'd need to be a part of the receiver rotation since it seems farfetched that he would contribute on special teams. A dropped touchdown in the second preseason game couldn't have helped his case.

It would be a great story, but it's far from a guarantee. And if Beckham makes it, it probably means 2023 third-round draft pick Jalin Hyatt does not (though both could end up not making the roster).

"I mean, I love Odell. I do," Giants head coach John Harbaugh said , via Giants Wire. "What he's doing, what he's fighting for, I don't know how it's going to turn out. It's going to turn out the way it turns out, based on what happens. But to see his fight, his determination, his humility. He's got his son in camp the other day, you know, he's doing it for his son. You know, that just, as a friend, that makes me really proud of him."

It was surprising to see Johnson play behind Travis Homer and Lew Nichols in the first preseason game. Johnson didn't appear in the game until the second half. That signifies he is fifth on the depth chart at best.

Johnson was an intriguing third-round pick a year ago. A mistake in the fourth quarter against Seattle in Week 2, mishandling a kickoff return that was recovered by the Seahawks in the end zone for a touchdown, was a blunder he never recovered from. He finished his rookie season with 69 rushing yards on 28 carries. A new coaching staff came in and Johnson was buried even further on the depth chart. Teams don't usually keep fifth-string tailbacks on the roster.

McCarthy, the 10th pick of the 2024 draft who struggled last season, is unlikely to be cut. He also might lose a competition with Carson Wentz to be the Vikings' backup quarterback and be on the third string by Week 1. If there is any player that desperately needs a trade and a new start, it's McCarthy. It can't be ruled out.

Coleman is another player who isn't getting cut, but would a trade be that surprising? When the team owner is assigning blame for drafting you , you're in trouble with the organization. Coleman, a 2024 second-round draft pick, still has time to become an impact receiver, whether it's in Buffalo or not.

Kirk missed almost all of training camp with a calf injury. The 49ers have a clear top three at receiver in Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling. Kirk doesn't have an obvious role, and that could put his roster spot in jeopardy. Kirk could also start the season on injured reserve.

Hamlin seems to have played his way onto the roster this summer, according to ESPN's Alaina Getzenberg . Still, he's a backup safety and 28 years old. Hamlin is likely to make the BIlls again, but he'll want the official news to make sure.

Dillon, who played four seasons with the Packers and last season with the Eagles, is trying to make the Panthers' roster. He has been working on special teams to help his case. That, and Chuba Hubbard's hamstring injury that kept him out for a lot of camp, could help him get a spot.

Appearing on the transaction wire is nothing new to the famously well-traveled Johnson. Johnson is 40 and always seems to find a backup job somewhere. The Bengals will have Joe Burrow and Joe Flacco on the active roster but likely have Johnson on speed dial or the practice squad.

Browns QB Dillon Gabriel or Taylen Green

Teams don't generally keep four quarterbacks. Green could be an exception because he's a stellar athlete who could be used in gadget roles. It seems likely the Browns keep Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders, Gabriel and Green, but it's unconventional and perhaps they would answer the phone if anyone calls about Dillon, a third-round pick last year.

Mingo was struggling as a young second-round pick for the Panthers when the Cowboys suddenly traded a fourth-round pick for him. It was panned by everyone and it hasn't worked out; he has just six catches for 71 yards since he was acquired during the 2024 season. The Cowboys' top four receivers are set, and Mingo is on the bubble to make the roster.

Elam was a first-round pick of the Bills in 2022. He didn't work out there and hasn't found footing elsewhere. He hasn't moved far up the Chiefs' depth chart and it seems likely he'll be a free agent again soon.

Colson seemed like a great fit as a third-round pick of the Chargers in 2024. He was joining his college coach, Jim Harbaugh. But Colson has had injury issues, has started only one game and has been playing with backups late in preseason games this year. It would be early to give up on him, but it's possible.

Dolphins WRs Jalen Reagor and Terrace Marshall Jr.

The Dolphins tried adding some receivers who were highly drafted a few years ago. Reagor was a former first-round pick and Marshall was a second-round pick, and neither panned out. They probably won't pan out in Miami either, but Reagor's ability as a returner gives him a shot to stick.

Saints QB Zach Wilson or Spencer Rattler

Will the Saints keep three quarterbacks? If not, either Wilson or Rattler have to go. Wilson had been behind Rattler for much of camp, but he started over Rattler in the second preseason game. Wilson and Rattler made mistakes in that game, so neither should feel like they're roster locks.

Tracy has been a productive back, but there's a new coaching staff and Tracy hasn't had a good camp or preseason. In the Giants' first preseason game he missed a pass block that led to a big hit on Jaxson Dart, and in the second preseason game he fumbled. The Giants signed Najee Harris, which makes the running back room even more crowded.

It seems unlikely that Rudolph will get cut, but it's also not typical for a team to keep four quarterbacks. Aaron Rodgers and recent draftees Will Howard and Drew Allar seem like locks. If Rudolph is on the roster it probably means the Steelers will be carrying four quarterbacks.

Cam Ward is the Titans' starter. Mitchell Trubisky is the backup. Maybe Levis stays on as the Titans' third quarterback, but a new coaching staff that didn't draft Levis would have to see the value in using a roster spot on him.

articles.title: New Fantasy Football 2026 Mock Draft Tips and Latest Consensus Rankings
articles.summary: The final week of the 2026 NFL preseason is underway, and real, meaningful football is nearly back. For fantasy enthusiasts, this means that we are entering the prime drafting window.
articles.body:
The final week of the 2026 NFL preseason is underway, and real, meaningful football is nearly back. For fantasy enthusiasts, this means that we are entering the prime drafting window.

Drafting after the August 30 roster cuts will be ideal, as managers will then have a clearer idea of player roles and roster statuses. Between now and then, though, they can prepare for their live drafts by running a few mocks and collecting the data.

Of course, to get the most out of mock drafts, it's best to execute them with a purpose. Here, you'll find some mock-drafting tips, a three-round mock conducted with FantasyPros' Mock Draft Simulator , and a look at FantasyPros ' latest consensus point-per-reception (PPR) rankings.

The biggest piece of advice we can offer about mock drafting is to take notes, track data, and pay close attention to where your favorite players are being taken. This information can help you create a personalized draft board that is more beneficial than even the latest consensus rankings.

The trick is to make sure that your mock draft parameters—roster makeup, scoring rules, flex options, etc.—match your actual draft perfectly. Under those guidelines, you may find that certain players you have circled pre-draft are going higher or lower than their consensus average draft position (ADP) might suggest.

When creating a personalized draft board, it's also a good idea to track any sleepers you've identified and wish to target. Has that high-upside rookie RB drifted upward from Round 12 toward Round 9? That's great information to have on draft day and can help prevent missing out on a prospect you love.

Experiment With Different Strategies, but Focus on RBs Early or Zero RB

Managers should try mock drafting from different positions, even if they know their draft slot, in order to get a feel for how other drafters may approach things. They should also try out different strategies to identify a preferred approach and a strong Plan B.

Whether you want to target a high-volume receiver like Ja'Marr Chase early in Round 1 or have your heart set on two elite RBs, there's a good chance that other managers will make that plan difficult.

In 2026, there's going to be a massive drop-off in RB talent after the initial wave. Players like James Cook, De'Von Achane, and Chase Brown form a solid group just under the elites—high-volume backs like Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson—but second-tier backs like Josh Jacobs and D'Andre Swift are far less appealing.

We'd recommend trying different strategies that yield at least one high-level RB within the first two rounds and two out of the first three. The WRs available in Rounds 4-8 are likely to have much more value than the RBs available in that range.

However, we'd also recommend trying a few zero-RB strategies as a backup plan. If there's an early run at the position, managers might benefit from snapping up top-tier WRs and TEs while looking for RB value after other starting lineups have been filled.

For example, getting RJ Harvey ( draft rank of 107) in Round 9 might yield far more value than taking Travis Etienne Jr. ( draft rank of 47) five rounds higher.

Lastly, it's important to run as many mock drafts as possible in order to get the most accurate collection of data.

Even one or two mocks can help managers get a feel for how they want to draft—and help get used to the panic of being on the clock right after your favorite player got sniped. However, a larger sample size will always paint a more accurate picture of where players are being valued and how strategies are working.

Kenneth Walker III, RB, Kansas City Chiefs

Omarion Hampton, RB, Los Angeles Chargers

Tetairoa McMillan, WR, Carolina Panthers

articles.title: Inspiring story on mental strength: “No one really sees pro athletes behind the scenes. They don't know how hard they work”- How Patrick Mahomes built a mindset beyond natural talent
articles.summary: NFL News: Patrick Mahomes became famous for throws that seemed almost impossible. Behind that effortless style, however, sits a lesson he learned long before be.
articles.body: Patrick Mahomes became famous for throws that seemed almost impossible. Behind that effortless style, however, sits a lesson he learned long before becoming an NFL superstar. As a child, Mahomes saw professional athletes prepare when nobody was watching. Those quiet hours changed how he viewed success, teaching him that natural ability can open the door, but repetition, preparation and discipline keep an athlete at the top.Patrick Mahomes learned about hard work before becoming an NFL starMahomes shared the insight in an ESPN profile published on October 10, 2018, during his spectacular first season as the Kansas City Chiefs' starting quarterback. Kevin Seifert's article, titled “‘Turbo Andy’ got his guy: Inside the Reid-Mahomes masterpiece,” examined the connection between Mahomes and head coach Andy Reid while also looking at the experiences that shaped the young quarterback.The most revealing part of the story had nothing to do with Mahomes' powerful arm.It began with his childhood.Mahomes grew up around professional baseball because his father, Pat Mahomes Sr., spent more than a decade pitching in Major League Baseball. During the summer, Patrick would accompany his father to big league ballparks. He got to see professional players up close, but the experience quickly became about more than watching stars perform.He watched them prepare.One example stayed with him. Alex Rodriguez, one of baseball's biggest stars at the time, would repeatedly hit balls off a tee before games. To a young Mahomes, that was striking. Rodriguez was already an elite hitter. Yet he still spent time working on one of the simplest drills in baseball.That observation shaped Mahomes' understanding of greatness.He later explained, “No one really sees pro athletes behind the scenes. They don't know how hard they work.”The larger point of his comment was clear. Fans usually see the finished product. They see the touchdown, the home run, the highlight and the celebration. They rarely see the repetitions that come first.For Mahomes, that distinction became an important part of his own approach.Alex Rodriguez showed Patrick Mahomes why basics matterThe lesson Mahomes took from Rodriguez was not simply that professional athletes work hard. It was that even the best players continue returning to the fundamentals.Mahomes specifically pointed to Rodriguez's use of a batting tee. The drill looked basic, especially for someone of Rodriguez's stature. But that was exactly why it mattered.Elite athletes do not abandon simple exercises once they become successful. They often become more committed to them.That idea is easy to overlook because professional sports are built around spectacular moments. A quarterback launches a 50-yard touchdown pass and fans remember the throw. They do not see the countless hours spent studying defensive schemes, reviewing film, repeating footwork or learning how to recognize patterns.Mahomes understood this difference early.His father's own routine reinforced the lesson. After games, Pat Mahomes Sr. would return to his notes and study opposing hitters. While Patrick might go play video games or spend time with friends, his father continued preparing.The contrast showed Mahomes that preparation does not end simply because the game is over.That mindset would later become part of his football routine.Patrick Mahomes applied the lesson to his own preparationBy the time Mahomes reached the NFL, he had already developed an appreciation for studying the details that most people never notice.In the ESPN profile, he explained that he carried the lessons from his childhood into his own film study. He described reviewing game plans repeatedly, including material that had already been covered, because familiarity should never become an excuse to stop paying attention.That approach mattered as Mahomes adjusted to the NFL.His talent was obvious. His arm strength was extraordinary. His ability to throw from different platforms made him one of the most exciting young quarterbacks in football.But Andy Reid and the Chiefs needed more than physical ability.During Mahomes' pre-draft visit to Kansas City in 2017, the coaching staff tested his ability to absorb information. Reid taught him a series of plays, formations, protections and calls. Mahomes then returned to the room and essentially recreated the offense on the whiteboard.Chiefs assistant Brad Childress later summed up the mentality that separates elite players from everyone else: “They're not great because they're great. They work to be great.”That observation fits closely with Mahomes' own childhood lesson.The hidden work behind Patrick Mahomes' successMahomes' career has since become filled with spectacular plays, records and championships. Yet the lesson from his early years remains relevant because it explains something that highlights cannot show.Greatness can look effortless from the outside.It rarely feels effortless to the person doing the work.Mahomes learned that from watching professional baseball players prepare when the cameras were not focused on them. Rodriguez did not need to prove that he was a great hitter every time he stepped onto a field. Instead, he kept refining the smallest parts of his craft.Mahomes adopted the same principle.His own preparation involves film study, repetition and attention to detail. He has spoken about reviewing material every day and making sure he understands every aspect of a game plan rather than assuming he already knows enough.That is perhaps the most powerful part of his message.Fans often see confidence. They see creativity. They see the no-look passes, the sidearm throws and the plays that appear to happen instinctively.Mahomes sees something else.He sees the work that makes those moments possible.His quote from the 2018 ESPN profile therefore carries a lesson that extends beyond football. Success often hides its own process. The strongest performers can make difficult things appear ordinary because they have repeated them so many times.That was the lesson a young Mahomes absorbed while watching his father and some of baseball's biggest stars.Years later, it became part of the foundation of his own career.The spectacular plays may be what make Patrick Mahomes famous. The unseen work is what helps explain why he can keep producing them.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Man who masqueraded as 49ers player facing federal charges in alleged wire fraud scheme that exploited women
articles.summary: He and another man are accused of defrauding at least 26 victims of more than $1.3 million, according to the U.S. Attorney's office in the District of Oregon...
articles.body:
A man who adopted "fictitious personas," one of which notably was that of a fake San Francisco 49ers player, is part of a duo that's been arrested and charged for defrauding several women of more than $1.3 million, according to the U.S. Attorney's office in the District of Oregon .

The FBI arrested 35-year-old Daejon Love and 18-year-old Taylor Jamie Chan on Monday in Boise, Idaho, where they were apprehended upon meeting at the Boise Airport. They're facing a pair of federal charges: conspiracy to commit wire fraud and wire fraud, as detailed in a statement released this week by the U.S. Attorney's office that references court documents.

Love, who the U.S. Attorney's office says repeatedly posed as a Niners player or as a wealthy real estate investor, and Chan, who the U.S. Attorney's office says acted as Love's financial adviser, allegedly accrued the aforementioned sum by exploiting at least 26 victims. Those are the ones the FBI has identified, and the bureau believes there are "many more."

The alleged scheme spanned four years, beginning in February 2022. Love and Chan targeted women in California, Oregon, Washington and Idaho, most of whom Love met through dating apps, prosecutors said. Love has used several names — including Jon Love, Daejon Love, Avril Lyto Love and Jordan Love — while carrying out the caper, per the U.S. Attorney's office.

"Love convinced many of the victims they were in sincere romantic relationships with Love, that he was a sophisticated investor, and that Chan was his investment adviser who helped Love grow a fortune worth tens of millions of dollars," the U.S. Attorney's Office statement said. "Love had romantic relationships with many of the victims and told them he wanted to build wealth and a future together. Love advertised nonexistent investment vehicles and claimed these investments would generate massive returns for both him and his victims."

"Love convinced many of the victims they were in sincere romantic relationships with Love, that he was a sophisticated investor, and that Chan was his investment adviser who helped Love grow a fortune worth tens of millions of dollars," the U.S. Attorney's Office statement said.

"Love had romantic relationships with many of the victims and told them he wanted to build wealth and a future together. Love advertised nonexistent investment vehicles and claimed these investments would generate massive returns for both him and his victims."

Phony bank and investment accounts and balances, created via phone applications, allegedly allowed Love to strengthen the validity of the ploy. Chan and Love even held three-way FaceTimes to flaunt falsified investment gains to whichever victim was on the call, according to the U.S. Attorney's office.

Victims sent Love and Chan money with the intent that it would be deployed for fruitful investments overseen by the tandem, prosecutors said.

"Once victims had no more money to invest, or if they asked too many questions, Love blocked communication with them but kept their money," the U.S. Attorney's office statement said.

"Of the victims identified and interviewed, none reported receiving any proceeds, returns on their principle, or investment account information, after sending Love and Chan money."

At the time of Love and Chan's arrest, Love was in Idaho to meet new victims, per investigators.

articles.title: Falcons QB Tua Tagovailoa booed by Dolphins fans as Miami pays price for failed relationship
articles.summary: Tua Tagovailoa completed 7 of 8 passes against his former team but still hasn't locked down the Atlanta Falcons starting job over Michael Penix Jr.
articles.body: As reunions go, Tua Tagovailoa’s return to South Florida as an Atlanta Falcon against his former Miami Dolphins teammates was not exactly a happy one. Dysfunctional is a better word for it. For six seasons, Tagovailoa and the Dolphins tried to make it work. They failed. DOLPHINS NOT GOING TO 'THROW IN THE TOWEL AND JUST REBUILD' BUT THAT COMES WITH HIGHER EXPECTATIONS Tagovailoa was set back by some coaches who didn’t like him and injuries that too often overshadowed him, so he never reached his goal of becoming the face of the franchise. And the Dolphins never came close to reaching the championship level they expected when they drafted Tagovailoa in the top five in 2020 and paid him like a top-five quarterback in 2024. The failures resulted in a divorce during the offseason and this exhibition game at Hard Rock Stadium was the first time the couple happened to be at the same place at the same time since the split. And guess what? Everybody believes they're better off after the separation. But no one is at this stage better off after the separation. DOLPHINS CONSULTANT TROY AIKMAN WILL BE LIMITED IN MNF ROLE LIKE RAIDERS MINORITY OWNER TOM BRADY IS ON FOX Tagovailoa is trying to earn a starting job with the Falcons and the fact he came into this game without yet having done so speaks to his failing since training camp began. Because Tagovailoa has basically been competing only against himself while Michael Penix Jr. has been limited in practices as he makes his way back from a 2025 knee surgery. And, yet, with his only significant competition sidelined and the path to the starting job clear, Tagovailoa hasn't been able to lock the job down. The Dolphins? They got rid of Tagovailoa this offseason despite the fact he would be costing them some $55 million in salary in 2026 alone. There's another bill coming next year. The Dolphins were so over this relationship they paid Tagovailoa to go away. And where has that left them? The Tagovailoa move was part of a systematic divestment from talent in order to "solve the salary cap problem" the previous administration got the franchise into. MIAMI DOLPHINS ENTER FULL REBUILD WITH MALIK WILLIS AT QUARTERBACK AND JEFF HAFLEY AS HEAD COACH The Dolphins are now perhaps the least talented team in the NFL as they prepare for a season in which they will be rebuilding for the 1,387th time in the past decade. So here we were on Friday night: Team Rebuild versus Quarterback Not Good Enough. The scene played out in front of a sparse crowd at Hard Rock that mustered enough emotion to boo for the quarterback they once believed would win them a championship. The Sadness Bowl. And, fittingly, nobody really won. Tagovailoa played well enough, completing 7 of 8 passes. But it wasn't actually good. The Dolphins, resting their talent-needy starting defense, fought with backups that will provide substandard depth this season. And the sparing between a QB who is lacking against backups who are lacking was, well, lacking. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tagovailoa completed 3 of 4 passes on his first drive, with the only incompletion on a throwaway. The Falcons scored a touchdown that drive. But that last paragraph reads more impressively than it looked because the dynamic 43-yard completion from Tagovailoa to Kyle Pitts that highlighted the drive was actually a 4-yard pitch on a screen that the tight end turned into a big run against a scattered defense. On his second drive, Tagovailoa fumbled the snap from center and the Dolphins recovered. And another drive later, running back Brian Robinson fumbled and, once again, the Miami defense recovered. So, good on the Miami defense that is going to get steamrolled once the regular-season begins. And good on Tagovailoa, who still hasn’t done enough to win the Falcons’ starting quarterback job despite facing little healthy competition until this week, when Penix Jr. was fully cleared to practice. Good on both. But not really that good. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

articles.title: New Seahawks owner Vinod Khosla defends Steelers fandom after saying he still watches all of their games
articles.summary: No one ask him about Super Bowl XL.
articles.body:
Vinod Khosla, the new owner of the Seattle Seahawks, might have a made the mistake of being too honest while introducing himself to his team's fanbase.

Speaking with reporters on Thursday, the day after the NFL's owners unanimously approved his $9.612 billion purchase of the Seahawks , Khosla discussed his past NFL fandom. Specifically, he confirmed he rooted for a team other than the Seahawks before buying them.

That team wasn't the San Francisco 49ers, whom Khosla purchased a 3% stake in alongside his son last year (which he will now be selling).

No, it's the Pittsburgh Steelers, the NFL's dominant team when Khosla entered the United States decades ago. He said still considers himself a fan of the team and watches every game:

"I happened to come to this country in '76 when the Steelers were winning Super Bowls, so actually I was originally, and still am, a big Steelers fan, also. Little known fact, but I still watch all the Steelers games too."

That one answer drew quite a bit of interest, so much so that Khosla decided to further explain himself on social media the next day. He insisted he will always want the Seahawks to win and complained about the media's reaction to his comments.

"Reporters will make every molehill into a mountain just to get column inches to write or video minutes. What's wrong with admitting my 1976-78 period in Pittsburgh (CMU) got me excited about the NFL? I still watch their games doesn't mean I won't unconditionally ALWAYS as owner, want the @Seahawks to win and have every edge up, EVERY TIME over every other team!!!! Zero questions!!! At the other end is a set of teams I always want to lose every advantage. But happy to have the sports writer getting more column inches and fill their pages. You are welcome. Apologies in advance for my very transparent style."

Khosla obviously wouldn't be the first person to have dual rooting interests in the NFL. We're just dealing with the rare owner who does not care if fans know he has another team he still loves. That's ultimately up to him, but you could forgive Seahawks fans for being a little more wary of what this era will look like.

Khosla's tenure as owner will ultimately be decided by the product on the field and the conduct of the organization. In the meantime, let's just hope he doesn't bring up Super Bowl XL too much in the Pacific Northwest.

articles.title: John Harbaugh Reveals If Odell Beckham Jr. Has Done Enough to Make NFL Roster After Giants Preseason
articles.summary: New York Giants coach John Harbaugh expressed confidence in Odell Beckham Jr. but came short of confirming the wide receiver has earned a roster spot after Friday's preseason finale against the New York Jets.
articles.body:
New York Giants coach John Harbaugh expressed confidence in Odell Beckham Jr. but came short of confirming the wide receiver has earned a roster spot after Friday's preseason finale against the New York Jets.

"I think he has done enough to make an NFL roster for sure," Harbaugh said Friday about Beckham (h/t Fox Sports' Ralph Vacchiano). "He's played well. He's gotten better as camp's gone along, and I think he deserves credit for that."

Landing spots for NFL players already cut

The Giants signed Beckham in June and will need to decide whether to keep him by the 53-man roster deadline this Sunday at 6 p.m. ET.

Harbaugh said Wednesday he thought this week had been Beckham's best of training camp.

Beckham followed that up Friday by making three catches on six targets for 53 yards in preseason action against the Jets. He also came close to what could have been a 73-yard touchdown after getting open for a deep ball from Jameis Winston.

"It would mean everything," Beckham said about potentially making the Giants roster on the in-game broadcast . "It would be my dream. This is where I started. There's no place I want to give my whole heart to, more than anything else in the world, is this place right here."

Beckham continued after the game: "I'm super grateful for the opportunity, and at this point, it's in God's hands.

"I know that I have a good feeling about myself. I feel like there's ball to be played, there's plays to be made."

Beckham, who will turn 34 in November, played three Pro Bowl seasons with the Giants between 2014 and 2016 before his career was derailed by injuries.

The wide receiver last played in the NFL during the 2024 season, during which he appeared in nine games but saw minimal usage with the Miami Dolphins.

He did not sign with any team during the 2025 season, which he started out by serving a six-game suspension for failing the NFL's performance-enhancing drug policy.

Beckham is now trying to make his NFL comeback in a wide receiver room that just lost receiver Calvin Austin III to a season-ending torn right ACL .

"It just means that the next guy steps up and fills that role. We have to readjust," Harbaugh said Wednesday about Austin's injury.

Harbaugh will now have to decide if Beckham's training camp and Austin's injury, combined with preseason struggles from Braxton Berrios, are enough to justify keeping Beckham around for when the Giants open the regular season Sept. 13 against the visiting Dallas Cowboys.

articles.title: 12 toughest cuts from our final Saints 53-man roster predictions
articles.summary: A couple of draft picks, rookie fan-favorites, and plucky veterans weren't able to catch on in our final New Orleans Saints 53-man roster predictions.
articles.body:
This year's NFL roster cuts deadline falls on 5 p.m. CT on Sunday, Aug. 30, giving all 32 teams a quick turnaround between their final preseason game and dozens of tough visits to the office. Like each of their rivals, the New Orleans Saints must cut their rosters down from 90 players to just 53 of them. It's one of the harshest days on the league's calendar.

Some decisions are more difficult than others. Guys have competed hard all summer, fighting through injuries and pushing against competition from other pros who want to make the cut just as badly as they do. But the reality is that just 53 players can make the team. Here were our toughest decisions in trying to predict how the Saints will approach roster cuts .

Wilson flashed the same potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick at times this summer, but those flashes were too few and far between for him to be our QB2 (at least so long as Spencer Rattler is around). Even if he can dress out on game days with the emergency QB3 rule, it's not worth burning a roster spot on him. It wasn't worth doing that for Jake Haener, either.

This isn't exactly another Boston Scott situation, but it's not far off from that, either. Neal just hasn't been able to stay healthy. He missed long stretches of his rookie year with hamstring issues and those same injuries have plagued him this summer. He may be a reliable third-down back with real chops in pass protection, but he simply hasn't been available enough to win a roster spot with those skills. Hopefully he can catch on with the practice squad or just heal up for a month or two on injured reserve.

Austin had one more target in team drills (22) than Means did (21) this summer, and his team-first attitude has won over some fans. But the additions the Saints have made in the receiving corps are pushing guys like him onto the practice squad. That's not a bad thing, in the big picture, but it's a setback for Austin as he tries to get his own career off the ground.

Bell has also been targeted 21 times throughout training camp, but he hasn't been quite as productive or consistent (six of those passes went his way in a single session). He's another good option for the practice squad as an experienced pro who knows the playbook well.

It's been another solid summer for Welch, who consistently drew targets in team drills throughout training camp and showcased soft hands in the preseason games, but he hasn't made enough strides as a blocker to make the cut. There's potential here if he could put everything together.

Simpkins was a fan-favorite last summer as a rookie free agent, and it looked like he could have taken a larger role on offense as Erik McCoy's backup after switching to center full-time. Instead, he's been bumped down the depth chart before losing the last week of practice while in concussion protocol. You'd like to get him back on the practice squad but this has still been a rough preseason for Simpkins.

Neither Smyth nor Tanner Brown were able to win the kicker competition this summer, but Smyth's status as an International Pathway Player means he can hang around on the practice squad without taking a roster spot. He has obvious talent, he just needs more experience. Another season of development could be good for him.

Two different coaching staffs have had plenty of time to evaluate Boyd at practice and chosen to play others ahead of him, even while he's graded out well in the preseason. For whatever reason the moments we've seen haven't carried over day-to-day, and this could be the end of the line for him in New Orleans despite a thin depth chart on the interior defensive line.

Heldman quickly built up a fanbase after notching a couple of sacks in the first preseason game; he just couldn't keep that momentum going. He spent most of the summer on the third-team defense and projects well as a fit for the practice squad. He did leave the Cowboys game late with an injury, so look out for an update on his status.

Rumph was a very important player in Brandon Staley's defense last season and it says a lot that he was brought back and cross-trained at off-ball linebacker after rushing off the edge. He's lost a lot of time to an ankle injury but likely would have made the team if healthy.

The numbers game just wasn't in Davison's favor. He's done everything asked of him on defense and special teams, but it hasn't been enough to separate himself from more-accomplished pros. He's another practice squad candidate if he clear waivers.

It's always disappointing to see a draft pick not make the team, even if he's a seventh rounder. There are just different expectations for guys who hear their name called during the event. Hall is a safe pick to return on the practice squad unless another team claims him off of waivers.
